R039-03.notes: Glucose rises only after ice touches the skin, so a frog that has not started freezing has much less blood glucose. B reverses the relationship, since glycogen has not yet been used. C is wrong because a frozen frog's heart has stopped. D is wrong because there is no ice yet. B is the main trap.

R039-04.notes: This item connects paragraph 4 to the mechanism in paragraph 3: more glycogen means more glucose can be made once freezing starts. A, B and D have no support in the passage or contradict it. Science checks out: Alaskan wood frogs in Costanzo/Lee studies had larger liver glycogen stores and fall urea accumulation, and they tolerated roughly -16 to -18 C, against roughly -3 to -6 C for southern/midwestern frogs.

R039-05.notes: The cell fluid loses water, so it is less diluted. A ('more focused') is the common-meaning trap, and C ('gathered in one place') is a plausible near-miss.
